title: "BECS in the pipeline"

## The ticket

Friday, 3:40 p.m. IT Operations has a routine patch queued for Monday night: a vendor-released
security update to the operating system on the application server running Lakeshore Blood
Center's Blood Establishment Computer Software (BECS). Medium-severity CVE, vendor advisory two
weeks old, the same patch already went out on eleven other Windows servers this month without
incident. Your systems administrator built the change ticket the way he builds every other one:
standard change, pre-approved patch window, rollback plan attached, done.

Your Quality Analyst rejects it an hour before the CAB (change advisory board) meeting. Not
"needs more testing" — rejected outright, with one line: "No BECS change deploys without a
validation impact assessment first. Standard change process doesn't apply here."

Your sysadmin is in your office five minutes later, annoyed. "It's an OS patch. We didn't touch
a single line of BECS's own code. Every other server in the building gets this exact same patch
without a three-week paper trail. Why does this one server get treated like we're installing a
new application?"

He's not wrong that it's the same patch. He's wrong about what server it's sitting on — and by
Monday's CAB, you're the one who has to explain the difference to both of them, and then explain
it again, in two sentences, to a CIO who's going to ask the same question your sysadmin just did.

## Why this rule exists — and the ITSM bridge

Here's the failure mode underneath your QA's rejection, stated plainly: BECS isn't a system that
*records* what happened during blood collection, testing, labeling, and release. Across the last
four modules, you've watched it *decide* — or gate the decision on — whether each of those steps
is allowed to proceed. A patch that changes how the operating system handles memory, threading, or
a shared library doesn't have to touch BECS's application code to change how BECS behaves. An OS
patch has, in real incidents across regulated industries, quietly altered timing, rounding, or
error-handling behavior in the software running on top of it — the kind of change nobody would
notice on a system that just stores data, and the kind of change that matters enormously on a
system that gates whether a unit of blood is allowed to reach a patient. Treat every change to that
server the same way you'd treat a routine patch anywhere else, and you've quietly removed the
review step that exists specifically to catch the case where "we didn't touch the code" turns out
to be false.

You already own the ITSM vocabulary for exactly this problem — it's just been aimed at service
availability and security, not at the product itself, and this module is the richest place in the
whole course to make that translation, because all three pieces of your existing fluency apply at
once.

**Change enablement under a validated state.** Your normal change model already scores risk and
routes accordingly — standard, normal, emergency, each with a different approval bar. BECS adds a
dimension your standard-change criteria were never built to catch: even a change with zero service
or security risk can still be a regulatory problem, because CGMP performance (whether that unit of
blood is safe to release) is a criterion your change advisory board doesn't normally have on its
checklist at all. That's what your QA's rejection is actually enforcing — not "this change is
risky" in your usual sense, but "this change touches a system that has to stay in a documented,
proven-reliable state, and nobody has yet shown that this patch doesn't move it out of that state."

**Service asset and configuration management.** BECS is a configuration item (CI) in your CMDB —
so is every system it interfaces with: the OS it runs on, the instrument interfaces feeding it test
results, the ICCBBA product code table module 3 already showed you being consumed as external
reference data. A normal CI record tracks owner, environment, dependencies, lifecycle state. A
BECS-linked CI carries one more attribute a normal CMDB entry doesn't: its *current validated
configuration* — the specific, documented version of hardware, OS, application code, and
interfaces that was shown to perform its critical functions reliably. Drift from that configuration
isn't just technical debt to schedule later. It's a compliance gap the moment it happens, whether
anyone opens a ticket for it or not.

**One incident, two tracks.** If a BECS malfunction ever lets something through that shouldn't
have — say, a defect that let a deferred donor register at a second site, or a timing bug that
released a unit before its quarantine gate should have opened — you don't have one incident to run
down. You have two, in parallel, with different owners and different clocks. IT incident
management gets the system back to a known-good state and closes when service is restored. A
separate track asks whether that malfunction is a **deviation**, potentially reportable to FDA as a
biological product deviation under 21 CFR 606.171 — the reporting obligation the
`risk-and-controls-vocabulary` foundation lesson already walked you through in full, including the
"may affect," not "did affect," standard that makes this determination unavoidable even when
nothing shipped. That track doesn't close when the ticket does. It closes when Quality has
documented the determination — even if the documented answer turns out to be "not reportable."

## The rule, in plain English — what BECS actually is

**BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software)** is software used by a blood establishment that
performs, or materially influences, a **critical function** in blood collection, processing,
testing, or distribution — a step where a software error, undetected, could directly affect
whether an unsafe or mislabeled product reaches a patient. That's the full definition this course
has been building toward one clause at a time. Here's the complete picture, in the exact language
each earlier module used:

1. **Module 1 (donor recruitment and screening):** BECS is "the system of record for donor
   eligibility and deferrals" — it holds the deferral registry an establishment must consult before
   ever collecting from a donor, and the record that an eligibility decision was actually made.
2. **Module 2 (collection and testing):** BECS is the gate. In that module's words, "no product
   carrying this donation's identifier moves past release, regardless of what's already happened to
   it physically, until BECS says the gate has opened" — a quarantine-status check, run
   automatically, that has to clear before any component derived from a donation can be released,
   shipped, or used.
3. **Module 3 (component processing and labeling):** BECS "controls whether a final label can
   print" — the system that has to hold current, correct product code and labeling data before it
   will let a barcode go onto a bag.
4. **Module 4 (storage, distribution, and hemovigilance):** BECS "drives inventory, shipping, and
   final disposition" — the system tracking where a released unit is, and what its final status
   becomes, right up until it's handed off to a hospital's own systems (its LIS, running
   compatibility testing and crossmatch, and its HIS, holding the clinical transfusion record) — the
   exact point where Lakeshore's visibility, and BECS's role, ends.

Put those four together and you get the real reason your QA's answer wasn't overcaution: BECS is
the single piece of software sitting underneath every regulated decision point this entire course
has walked through — who's allowed to donate, what's allowed to leave quarantine, what's allowed to
print on a label, and what's allowed to ship. There is no equivalent system anywhere else in a
typical enterprise stack, because there is no equivalent set of decisions anywhere else in the
business with this direct a line to patient safety.

That's *why* FDA treats software performing these functions differently from ordinary IT
infrastructure — and it happens on two overlapping legal footings, not one:

**First, CGMP applies to the function, not just to the person or machine performing it.** 21 CFR
606.100(b) requires written procedures "for all steps in the collection, processing, compatibility
testing, storage, and distribution of blood and blood components" — donor eligibility criteria,
donor-to-unit identity linking, labeling procedures, final disposition. When BECS performs or gates
one of those steps instead of a person doing it on paper, the software inherits the same CGMP
expectation the regulation has always applied to the step itself: it has to work reliably, and
Lakeshore has to be able to prove it, on demand, the same way it has to prove a phlebotomist
followed the DHQ (donor history questionnaire) correctly.

**Second, for software whose function goes further — actually making or controlling the release
decision, not just recording one a person made — FDA's authority reaches beyond CGMP procedure and
into medical device law.** Software that performs functions like this can meet the FD&C Act's
definition of a medical device in its own right, which for many BECS products means the vendor had
to clear it through FDA's premarket device review process (a 510(k) submission) before it could
even be sold into the U.S. market — the same regulatory gate a physical diagnostic instrument goes
through, applied to software making a release decision instead of a physical test result. You don't
need device-classification law to run Lakeshore's IT function; you need to know that this second
footing exists, because it's the reason your BECS vendor isn't just another SaaS vendor — they're a
regulated manufacturer of the software itself, subject to their own FDA obligations for defects and
design changes, quite apart from anything Lakeshore does on its end.

FDA has also published guidance specifically on this topic — a document commonly referenced in the
industry as **"Blood Establishment Computer System Validation in the User's Facility,"** issued by
FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER). *A verification note, in the same spirit
as the `regulatory-landscape-orientation` foundation lesson's handling of an unreachable guidance
page: this session could not fetch FDA's own guidance-document page to confirm the current version
and exact issue date, so none is quoted here — confirm the current version from FDA's guidance
database before citing a specific date in a real Lakeshore document.* What that guidance covers —
the actual validation methodology, IQ/OQ/PQ (installation, operational, and performance
qualification), and the GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing Practice) risk-based framework the
industry commonly uses to structure it — is deliberately **not** this module's job. That's the
entire subject of Track 3, `csv-and-becs`, later in the curriculum. This module's job stops at
*why* that heavier process exists; it doesn't teach *how* to run it.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(b) | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph b" | Written SOPs required for all CGMP steps in collection, processing, testing, storage, and distribution. | The regulatory floor BECS inherits the moment it performs one of these steps instead of a person — the reason "we didn't touch the application code" doesn't end the analysis for an OS patch. |
| 21 CFR 11.10(a) | "Eleven point ten, paragraph a" | Part 11 (electronic records and signatures) requires "validation of systems to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance." | Named here for the concept only — this is where "maintaining a validated state" traces to in the regulation itself. Part 11's full electronic-records framework (audit trails, ALCOA+) gets its complete treatment in Track 3. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(b)(1)(ii) | "Six-oh-six point one-seven-one, paragraph b, sub-one, clause ii" | An "unexpected or unforeseeable event" that "may affect" the safety, purity, or potency of a distributed product is reportable as a biological product deviation. | The test that turns a BECS software defect into a potential BPDR (biological product deviation report), not just a closed incident ticket — already covered in full in `risk-and-controls-vocabulary`. |

## The actual text

The SOP requirement, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md` — the same regulation two
earlier foundation lessons already grounded, now applied to software performing the step instead of
a person:

> Establishments must establish, maintain, and follow written standard operating procedures for all
> steps in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage, and distribution of blood and
> blood components for allogeneic transfusion, autologous transfusion, and further manufacturing
> purposes...

Nothing in that sentence carves out an exception for "the step is performed by software instead of a
person." A donor-eligibility determination, a quarantine release, a label-printing control, a
disposition decision — each one is a CGMP step named directly in 606.100(b)'s own subparagraphs
across the four modules you've just recapped, and each one is a step BECS performs or gates.

The validated-state concept itself, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/11.10.md`:

> (a) Validation of systems to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance, and
> the ability to discern invalid or altered records.

Read that sentence the way your QA reads it: BECS doesn't get a one-time validation and then a free
pass forever. It has to keep demonstrating "consistent intended performance" — which is exactly what
an unreviewed OS patch puts at risk, whether or not the patch itself is dangerous. This single clause
is as deep as this module goes into Part 11; the full electronic-records framework built on top of
it is Track 3's job.

And the reportability standard, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.171.md` — already the full
subject of the `risk-and-controls-vocabulary` foundation lesson, worth one more read with BECS
specifically in mind:

> (b)(1)(ii) Represents an unexpected or unforeseeable event that may affect the safety, purity, or
> potency of that product...

A mislabeled bag and a software defect that mis-executes a labeling decision "may affect" a product
the same way, on the same regulatory test. The medium is different; the reportability test isn't.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reviewing Lakeshore's change history for the BECS application
server doesn't ask whether the patch was applied successfully. They ask for three specific
artifacts, and a gap in any one of them is a finding on its own, regardless of whether the patch
itself ever caused a problem.

**The validation impact assessment for this specific change** — a documented determination, made
*before* deployment, of whether this patch could plausibly affect BECS's critical functions, signed
by someone with the authority to make that call. "We patch these servers every month with no
issues" is a track record, not an assessment. The assessment has to exist for *this* patch, on *this*
system, every time — even when the eventual conclusion is "no meaningful risk, proceed."

**The change control record showing Quality's sign-off**, not just IT's. For a normal enterprise
system, IT approval closes a standard change. For BECS, the record an inspector expects to see
includes Quality as a required approver in the workflow itself, not a courtesy notification after
the fact — the same distinction between "informed" and "owns a sign-off" that separates a real
control from a documentation gap.

**Vendor qualification and change-notification records** — proof that Lakeshore's BECS vendor is
contractually obligated to notify Lakeshore of updates *before* they're pushed, and evidence that
Lakeshore actually reviews and tests vendor-initiated changes rather than absorbing them silently.
You've already seen what happens without this control: module 3's ICCBBA product-code-table
push — a vendor update Lakeshore's own BECS applied mid-shift, with no advance review, that put
roughly forty units' printed barcodes one revision behind before anyone caught it. That wasn't a
labeling failure at its root. It was a vendor-change-governance failure that happened to surface as
a labeling problem, and it's the single clearest argument in this course for why vendor
qualification records matter as much for BECS as validation records do.

## Common traps

**"It's just a patch, not a new feature, so it doesn't need review."** This is your sysadmin's
position, and it's the single most common gap FDA investigators find in BECS change records. The
regulation doesn't distinguish "feature work" from "maintenance work" — 11.10(a)'s "consistent
intended performance" standard applies to any change that could plausibly affect it, and an
underlying OS patch is exactly the kind of change that can shift behavior without anyone intending
it to. Size and intent of the change aren't the test; effect on validated behavior is.

**"BECS is IT's system — Quality doesn't need to be in the change control loop for it."** Backwards.
BECS is the one system in the building where Quality's sign-off is *more* load-bearing than IT's,
not less, precisely because the thing at risk from a bad change isn't service availability — it's
whether a critical CGMP function keeps working correctly. Routing a BECS change through IT's normal
approval chain alone, with Quality as an afterthought, is the exact gap your QA's rejection in this
scenario was built to close.

**"A security patch and a validated-state change are two different categories of risk."** They're
not — they're two different *lenses* on the same underlying question: did anything change about how
this system behaves? A security patch that changes memory handling, library versions, or timing
behavior can affect BECS's critical-function performance just as much as a change explicitly labeled
"functional update," even though it was never intended to touch application logic. Treating "it's a
security fix" as automatically lower-risk than "it's a feature change" ignores that validated-state
risk and security risk are assessed on completely different criteria — a change can be low-risk on
one and genuinely uncertain on the other.

## What this means for your job

- **Build a BECS-specific change category into your change model, separate from "standard" and
  "emergency."** Every change to BECS itself, or to the OS and infrastructure it runs on, routes
  through a validation impact assessment and requires Quality's sign-off as a blocking approval —
  not a notification, an approval — before it deploys, regardless of how routine it looks.
- **Ask your Quality Analyst, before any BECS change goes to CAB, whether the impact assessment is
  written down, not just discussed.** "We talked it through and it seemed fine" is not the artifact
  an inspector expects to find; a documented assessment, even a short one, is.
- **Put vendor change notification in the contract, not in good faith.** Ask your BECS vendor
  directly: what's their obligation to tell Lakeshore *before* pushing an update, and what's
  Lakeshore's window to review and test it first? If the answer is vague, that's a vendor-management
  gap worth escalating before the next ICCBBA-table-style surprise, not after.
- **Treat a BECS incident as opening two tickets, not one, every time.** The IT incident closes when
  service is restored. The quality determination — was this potentially a 606.171 event — closes
  only when Quality documents an answer, and your job is making sure that second ticket never quietly
  gets forgotten because the first one closed cleanly.
- **When you brief your CIO on why BECS can't move at ordinary IT speed, lead with the function, not
  the paperwork.** "It's regulated" undersells it and invites pushback. "This software decides
  whether a unit of blood is safe to release — the same decision a person used to make by hand under
  the same CGMP rule — so a change to it gets the same scrutiny a change to that decision would" is
  the two-sentence version that actually lands.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your Quality Analyst tells the vendor that "FDA regulation requires BECS validation to follow the GAMP 5 framework with IQ, OQ, and PQ phases." Accurate?

Not quite, and this is worth catching before it goes in a vendor contract. FDA regulation (21 CFR
11.10(a), and 606.100(b) for the underlying CGMP steps) requires that systems performing these
functions be validated — "accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance" — but it doesn't
name a specific methodology in the regulatory text. GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing Practice,
published by ISPE) and the IQ/OQ/PQ (installation/operational/performance qualification) structure
are industry-practice tier: the near-universal, defensible way the industry demonstrates it met the
regulatory standard, not language lifted from the CFR itself. This is the same regulation-versus-
guidance-versus-industry-practice mistake the `regulatory-landscape-orientation` foundation lesson
opened the whole curriculum with, showing up again at the end of it. Track 3 (`csv-and-becs`) is
where you'll learn what GAMP 5 and IQ/OQ/PQ actually require in practice.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your sysadmin argues the OS patch "doesn't need Quality's sign-off because we're not changing any BECS application code, only the operating system underneath it." Correct?

No. 11.10(a)'s "consistent intended performance" standard is about BECS's actual behavior, not about
which layer of the stack a change touches. An OS-level patch can alter timing, memory handling, or
error behavior in ways that change how the application running on top of it performs, even with zero
lines of BECS's own code modified. The validation impact assessment exists precisely to make that
determination *before* deployment — "we didn't touch the application" is an input to that assessment,
not a substitute for it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A BECS defect briefly lets a unit's quarantine status show "released" one screen refresh before all test results are actually in. Someone notices within the hour; nothing ships. Does this need a 606.171 reportability determination?

Yes, the determination itself is required — same "may affect," not "did affect," standard from the
`risk-and-controls-vocabulary` foundation lesson, now applied to software instead of a label. On
these facts, since nothing was distributed, 606.171(b)(3)'s distributed-product trigger likely isn't
met, so the likely conclusion is "not reportable." But that conclusion has to be reached, documented,
and filed by Quality — not assumed because the defect was caught quickly and nothing shipped. An
undocumented "no harm done" is the same gap here that it was for the label mix-up in that earlier
lesson, just wearing a software defect instead of a physical one.
:::

## Where this goes next

That's `blood-center-operations` — the whole course, done. Five modules walked one unit of blood
from a donor's eligibility interview through collection, testing, quarantine, component
processing, labeling, storage, shipping, and a hospital transfusion service, naming the regulated
step at every stage and, in this module, gathering every place BECS touched that path into one
picture: eligibility, release, labeling, and disposition, plus where its visibility stops at the
hospital's own LIS and HIS.

Two places pick up threads this module deliberately left open. **Track 3, `csv-and-becs`**, is
where the validation methodology this module only named — GAMP 5, IQ/OQ/PQ, the V-model, and what a
real validation impact assessment actually contains — gets taught in full; that's the natural next
stop for anyone who wants to turn this module's "why" into a working "how." **Track 2,
`quality-system-essentials`**, is where change control and deviation management — the CAPA process,
the mechanics of a BPDR filing, and how a quality council actually runs — get their own complete
treatment, beyond what this course's foundation lesson and this module's incident-track framing
covered. Neither is the immediate next build; both are where the threads this course opened are
waiting when you're ready to pull on them.
